mainTopic: יאוש שלא מדעת is settled like אביי; wind-fallen dates; and whether a trampled סימן or the place of loss counts as a סימן.
overview: The גמרא finishes its long test of the argument between אביי and רבא about יאוש שלא מדעת (giving up hope before the owner even knows the item is lost). A proof from the laws of הכשר is rejected. The פסוק of כי יותן, as רב פפא explains it, requires the wetting to happen with the owner's knowledge, and that is a special rule for הכשר alone. Then a פסוק about an item swept away by a river shows that an item lost only to its owner must be returned even when it has no סימן. That refutes רבא, and the הלכה follows אביי, one of the six cases of יע"ל קג"ם. רב אחא בריה דרבא then asks how we may eat dates blown down by the wind. רב אשי answers that the owner gives up on them in advance, because creatures eat them. Those dates are forbidden, though, when the land is known to belong to orphans or the trees are fenced in. Next the גמרא turns to bundles found in a public area. רבה and רבא argue whether a סימן likely to be trampled counts, and whether the place where an item was lost counts as a סימן. Each of them reads a ברייתא about bundles and sheaves according to his own view, and רבה's explanation continues on the next amud.

steps.title: End of the ברייתא: dried produce does not become susceptible
steps.stepSummary: The last words of the ברייתא rule that if the dew dried before the owner was happy about it, the produce is not under the law of כי יותן.
steps.simpleTranslation: [If the produce dried before he found out, even though he was happy afterward,] it is not under the law of 'when water is placed.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a ברייתא it began quoting just before this. The last line says that if the dew dried first, the owner's later happiness does not make the produce able to become טמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first half of the ברייתא said that dew falling on produce, when the owner is happy about it, counts as הכשר. This second half says that once the produce dried before he knew, his happiness comes too late. This ruling is what the גמרא will try to use as a proof in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: 'When [water] is placed' (ויקרא 11:38). The law that wet produce can become טמא.
Making food able to receive טומאה by getting it wet with a liquid.

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'בכי יותן' is not a bad thing for the owner in the sense of a sin. It simply means the produce can now become טמא if it touches something טמא.

phrases.english: They are not under the law of 'when [water] is placed.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a ברייתא that the גמרא started quoting earlier on the דף, as a test case for יאוש שלא מדעת.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Produce that dried before the owner was happy about the dew is not considered wetted with his approval, so it is not susceptible to טומאה.

steps.title: Trying to prove that later approval does not reach back
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the reason for the ruling is that we do not say 'since he is happy now, he was happy from the start.' This would be a proof against רבא about יאוש שלא מדעת.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason? Is it not because we do not say: since it has become clear that he is happy with it now, he was also happy with it from the beginning?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why dried produce is not affected. It suggests a reason that would decide the יאוש argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא holds that יאוש שלא מדעת counts, because once the owner finds out he will give up hope, so we treat him as having given up from the start. The ברייתא seems to say the opposite: approval that shows up later does not reach back to the time before he knew. That supports אביי.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter has become revealed. Later information shows what was true all along.
He is happy with it, it suits him.

steps.whyThisMatters: The idea that later knowledge shows what was true from the start is exactly what רבא needs to make יאוש שלא מדעת work.

phrases.english: What is the reason?
Is it not because we do not say
since the matter has been revealed
that now he is happy with it,
from the beginning he was also happy with it?

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא מַאי? לָאו מִשּׁוּם דְּלָא אָמְרִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws a general principle from the ברייתא's ruling and applies it to the יאוש dispute.
steps.raayaObject: That יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש, as אביי holds, against רבא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא ruling that later happiness about dew does not count once the produce has dried.

steps.title: Rejected: הכשר is different because the פסוק says 'when one places'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. הכשר has its own rule from the written word כי יתן, which needs the owner to place the water. So it says nothing about יאוש.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because it is written 'when one places,' meaning only when he places it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the proof. The ruling about dried produce comes from a special detail in the פסוק, not from a general rule about later approval.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word in the פסוק is spelled so that it can be read יִתֵּן, 'he places,' which points to the owner's own action. So produce that dried before he did or approved anything fails for a reason unique to הכשר. That reason does not apply to יאוש, which has no such פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different there. A standard way to reject a comparison.
'When one places.' The written spelling of the word in the פסוק.

phrases.english: It is different there, for it is written 'when one places.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 11:38. It's spelled without a ו, so it can be read יִתֵּן, 'he places.'

phrases.english: [It is not susceptible] until he places [the water].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought in step 2.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof from הכשר to יאוש entirely. It does not decide the יאוש question itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ruling in the ברייתא comes from a word in the פסוק that applies only to הכשר, not from a general rule about later approval.

steps.title: Challenge: then dew should not work in the first clause either
steps.stepSummary: If הכשר needs the owner to place the water himself, then the first half of the ברייתא, where dew fell on its own, should not count either.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the first clause too [should not be susceptible]!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave. If 'he places' is needed, dew that fell by itself should never make produce susceptible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first clause said that dew falling on produce, when the owner is happy, does count as הכשר. But nobody placed that dew. So reading the פסוק as 'he must place it' seems to contradict the ברייתא's own first half.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. Introduces a problem that follows from the last answer.
The first clause of a משנה or ברייתא.

phrases.english: If so, the first clause too [should be ruled not susceptible]!
phrases.notes: The first clause is where dew fell and the owner was happy, even though he never put the water there himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 3 by pointing to the ברייתא's first clause.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 3 that הכשר requires the owner to place the water himself.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first clause of the same ברייתא counts dew that fell by itself as הכשר, which no one placed. So 'he places' cannot be required literally.

steps.title: Answer: the first clause follows רב פפא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the first clause is explained by רב פפא's teaching, which it is about to quote.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is according to רב פפא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a short answer: the first clause fits רב פפא's view. This line sets up the next steps, where רב פפא's teaching is quoted in full.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of throwing out the 'he places' idea, the גמרא refines it using רב פפא. His teaching will show that the owner does not have to place the water himself, but the wetting has to be with his knowledge.

keyTerms.meaning: In line with רב פפא's teaching.

phrases.english: There, it is according to רב פפא.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts answering the challenge of step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings in an outside teaching (רב פפא) that refines how the פסוק is read.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The questioner thought that 'כי יתן' means the owner himself must place the water.
steps.terutzMaskana: Following רב פפא, the water does not have to be placed by the owner, as long as it comes with his knowledge, as the next steps explain.

steps.title: רב פפא's contradiction: written יתן, read יותן
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא points out that the word is written as כי יתן ('when one places') but read as כי יותן ('when it is placed'), and asks how the two fit together.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב פפא pointed out a contradiction: it is written 'when one places,' and we read 'when it is placed'! How can this be?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes רב פפא's question about the spelling and the reading of the word in the פסוק. This sets up his answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The spelling (כתיב) suggests the owner must put the water on himself. The traditional reading (קרי) suggests any water landing on the produce counts. רב פפא asks how both can be true at once.

keyTerms.meaning: He pointed out a contradiction between two sources.
It is written. How the word is spelled in the ספר תורה.
We read. How the word is traditionally pronounced.
How can this be? Asks how two conflicting things fit together.

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two forms. יִתֵּן means 'he places' (the owner acts). יוּתַּן means 'it is placed' (it can happen by itself).

phrases.english: For רב פפא pointed out a contradiction:
It is written 'when one places,'
and we read 'when it is placed'!
How can this be?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the teaching of רב פפא that step 5 referred to.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the written form 'he places' and the read form 'it is placed' fit together in one law.

steps.title: רב פפא's answer: 'it is placed' must be with knowledge, like 'he places'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא explains that יותן must be like יתן. Just as placing water yourself is done knowingly, water that lands on its own counts only if it happens with the owner's knowledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: We need 'it is placed' to be like 'one places.' Just as 'one places' is with knowledge, so too 'it is placed' must be with knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא answers his own question. This settles both the challenge about the first clause and why the proof about יאוש fails.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The reading יותן allows water that falls by itself, like dew. The spelling יתן adds a condition: it must be with the owner's knowledge and approval. That is why happy-about-dew counts, but dew that dried before he knew does not. This rule comes from the פסוק, so it cannot be used to decide יאוש שלא מדעת.
steps.whatToRemember: For הכשר, the water does not have to be placed by the owner (יותן), but it must happen with his knowledge (יתן). This is a special rule learned from the פסוק. So the ruling about dried produce cannot prove anything about יאוש שלא מדעת. The גמרא then tries a different proof in step 8, and that proof does decide the argument against רבא (step 10).
steps.whyThisMatters: It answers the challenge of step 4 and confirms the rejection in step 3. Knowledge is a requirement built into the פסוק of הכשר, not a general rule that also covers יאוש.

phrases.english: We require 'when it is placed' to be similar to 'when one places.'
Just as 'one places' is with knowledge,
so too 'when it is placed' must also be with knowledge.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב פפא's question in step 6, which completes the answer to step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The read form allows water placed by any means. The written form requires that it happen with the owner's knowledge.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Dew counts as הכשר only when it lands with the owner's knowledge and approval. This rule comes from the פסוק itself, so no proof can be drawn from it about יאוש שלא מדעת.

steps.title: A verse about an item swept away by a river
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי ישמעאל בן יהוצדק, learns from a פסוק that an item lost to everyone, like one swept away by a river, may be kept by the finder. An item lost only to its owner must be returned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי ישמעאל בן יהוצדק: How do we know that a lost item swept away by a river may be kept? Because the פסוק says 'every lost item of your brother which is lost from him and you have found it.' This means an item lost to him but still findable by people must be returned. An item lost to him and to everyone else is excluded.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source to settle the argument between אביי and רבא. This step lays out the source; the next step draws the proof from it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says 'lost from him and you found it,' meaning the item is lost only to the owner but anyone can still find it. An item swept away by a river is lost to the whole world, so it is excluded from the duty to return it. That gives us two groups: items you may keep (lost to all) and items you must return (lost only to the owner).

keyTerms.meaning: permitted (here: the finder may keep it)
available to be found by anyone

phrases.english: Come and hear

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק:
phrases.english: that Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yishmael ben Yehotzadak:
From where do we know about a lost item that a river swept away
that it is permitted?
phrases.notes: He means the finder is allowed to keep it.

phrases.english: As it is written: "And so shall you do with his donkey
and so shall you do with his garment
and so shall you do with every lost item of your brother
which is lost from him, and you have found it."
Something that is lost from him
but can still be found by any person must be returned;
excluded is this, which is lost from him
and cannot be found by any person.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן יְהוֹצָדָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from הכשר was rejected (Steps 3–7), the גמרא tries a new proof from a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: The argument between אביי and רבא about יאוש שלא מדעת
steps.raayaSupportSource: דברים 22:3, as explained by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי ישמעאל בן יהוצדק

steps.title: The forbidden case matches the permitted case
steps.stepSummary: Just as an item lost to everyone may be kept whether or not it has a סימן, an item lost only to its owner must be returned whether or not it has a סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The forbidden case is like the permitted case. Just as in the permitted case the finder may keep the item whether or not it has a סימן, so too in the forbidden case he may not keep it, whether or not it has a סימן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the actual proof from the פסוק by comparing the forbidden case to the permitted case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An item with no סימן is one the owner will surely give up on once he finds out it is lost. Even so, the פסוק forbids keeping it, as long as he has not yet given up. So giving up hope that has not happened yet, because he does not know, does not count. That is exactly what רבא denied.

keyTerms.meaning: the forbidden case: an item you may not keep
the permitted case: an item you may keep
an identifying mark that lets the owner prove the item is his

phrases.english: And the forbidden case is like the permitted case:
just as in the permitted case
whether it has a sign
or does not have a sign, it is permitted,
so too in the forbidden case,
whether it has a sign
or does not have a sign, it is forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the proof from the פסוק quoted in Step 8.
steps.raayaObject: Whether יאוש שלא מדעת counts as יאוש
steps.raayaSupportSource: The comparison between the forbidden and permitted cases in the פסוק: an item without a סימן is still forbidden.

steps.title: רבא is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares that רבא's view has been firmly disproven.
steps.simpleTranslation: The refutation of רבא is a true refutation!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא announces that the proof works, and רבא's opinion cannot stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the פסוק forbids keeping an item without a סימן before the owner knows it is lost, יאוש שלא מדעת does not count. That is אביי's view, so רבא is disproven.

phrases.english: The refutation of Rava is a refutation!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: States the outcome of the proof in Steps 8–9.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש; רבא is refuted.

steps.title: The הלכה follows אביי in six cases
steps.stepSummary: The הלכה follows אביי in the six cases remembered by the letters יע"ל קג"ם, and this is one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה follows אביי in the cases of יע"ל קג"ם.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the practical ruling: here we follow אביי, even though usually we follow רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally, when אביי and רבא argue, the הלכה follows רבא. The letters יע"ל קג"ם are a memory aid for the six cases where we follow אביי instead. The י stands for יאוש שלא מדעת, the case we are learning.

keyTerms.meaning: a memory aid: each letter stands for a case where the halacha follows אביי

steps.whatToRemember: יאוש שלא מדעת does not count as יאוש. This is one of the rare cases where the הלכה follows אביי against רבא.

phrases.english: And the halacha follows Abaye
in Ya'al Kagam.
phrases.notes: Each letter stands for one case where we follow אביי. The י is our case, יאוש שלא מדעת.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns the refutation of רבא into a practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows אביי: יאוש שלא מדעת is not יאוש.

steps.title: How can we eat dates blown down by the wind?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרבא asks רב אשי: now that רבא is disproven, how may we eat dates the wind knocked off a tree? The owner may not know they fell.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בריה דרבא said to רב אשי: Now that רבא has been disproven, how do we eat dates blown down by the wind?
steps.whatsHappening: Using the new ruling, רב אחא challenges a common practice: people pick up and eat wind-fallen dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner usually does not know which dates fell, so any giving up would be יאוש שלא מדעת. Under אביי's view that does not count. So it seems eating such dates should be forbidden, yet people do it.

keyTerms.meaning: dates knocked down by the wind

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי:
phrases.english: Rav Acha the son of Rava said to Rav Ashi:
And now that Rava has been refuted,
these dates blown down by the wind,
how do we eat them?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרָבָא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּאִיתּוֹתַב רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the new ruling against a common practice.
steps.kashyaTarget: The common practice of eating wind-fallen dates
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The owner doesn't know which dates fell, so any giving up is יאוש שלא מדעת, which no longer counts. So the dates should be forbidden.

steps.title: The owner gives up on fallen dates from the start
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that bugs and creeping creatures eat fallen dates, so the owner gives up on them in advance.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Since there are bugs and crawling creatures that eat them, the owner gives up on them from the very beginning.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי explains that wind-fallen dates are not a case of יאוש שלא מדעת at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner knows ahead of time that dates fall and get eaten by creatures, so he gives up on them in his mind before they even fall. This is real, knowing יאוש, so the dates may be eaten even under אביי.
steps.whatToRemember: Wind-fallen dates may be eaten because the owner gives up on them knowingly, ahead of time. It is not a case of יאוש שלא מדעת.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Since there are bugs and crawling creatures
that eat them,
from the start he gives up hope on them.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא שְׁקָצִים וּרְמָשִׂים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב אחא's challenge from Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: there is real, knowing יאוש here
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Wind-fallen dates are a case of יאוש שלא מדעת, so they should be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner expects creatures to eat fallen dates, so he gives up on them knowingly in advance, and they are permitted.

steps.title: What if the fallen dates belong to orphans?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא challenges רב אשי's answer: יתמי (minor orphans) cannot give up ownership, so how can anyone eat their fallen dates?
steps.simpleTranslation: Orphans are not able to give up their property. So what do we do?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא pushes back on רב אשי's last answer. Giving up in advance only works for an owner who is legally able to give up ownership, and young orphans are not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said the owner gives up on fallen dates ahead of time, because bugs will eat them. But a minor's יאוש does not count, since minors cannot let go of property. So if the tree might belong to יתמי, eating the dates should still be a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: People legally able to give up or let go of their rights

phrases.aramaic: יַתְמֵי דְּלָאו בְּנֵי מְחִילָה נִינְהוּ, מַאי?
phrases.english: Orphans, who are not able to give up their rights, what is the law?

steps.triggerLanguage: יַתְמֵי דְּלָאו בְּנֵי מְחִילָה נִינְהוּ, מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's answer in step 13 by raising an owner who cannot give up ownership.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אשי's claim that the owner gives up on fallen dates in advance
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Giving up in advance needs an owner who is able to give up. Minor orphans are not, so the explanation fails for their trees.

steps.title: We don't assume a field belongs to orphans
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that we do not assume an ordinary field belongs to יתמי, so we may follow the normal case.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: We do not assume that a field is land belonging to orphans.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers that we don't worry about orphans unless we have a reason to. A regular field is assumed to have a regular adult owner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Most fields are not owned by orphans, so the law follows the common situation. The worry about orphans would only matter if we knew the land was theirs.

keyTerms.meaning: A field or valley; open farmland
We assume; we treat as the default

phrases.english: He said to him:
We do not assume a field to be land of orphans.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: בָּאגָא בְּאַרְעָא דְיַתְמֵי לָא מַחְזְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 14.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Following the usual case: the rare possibility is not assumed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any tree might belong to יתמי, so fallen dates should always be forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: We don't assume orphan ownership without reason, so ordinary fallen dates are allowed.

steps.title: Known orphans' land, or fenced trees
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא asks about two cases: trees known to belong to orphans, and trees surrounded by a fence.
steps.simpleTranslation: If it is already known to be theirs, what is the law? If there is a fence, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא asks about two harder cases. These set up רב אשי's next answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first case removes רב אשי's last answer, because here we do know the land belongs to orphans. The second case removes the reason for giving up in advance, because a fence keeps the bugs and creeping creatures out.

keyTerms.meaning: Already established; known to be so
A fence or enclosure around the trees

phrases.english: If it is already established as theirs, what is the law?
A fenced area, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 15 by removing the conditions that allowed the dates.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether fallen dates are allowed when the land is known to be orphans', or when fences keep the bugs away

steps.title: In those cases the dates are forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי rules that in both cases the fallen dates are forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: They are forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers simply: in both of these cases, you may not eat the dates.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each case takes away the reason the dates were allowed. With known orphan land, no valid יאוש is possible. With a fence, the owner has no reason to give up. So the dates stay the owner's.
steps.whatToRemember: Fallen dates are normally allowed, because the owner gives up on them in advance. They are forbidden when the land is known to belong to orphans, or when a fence protects them.

phrases.english: He said to him: They are forbidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers both questions of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: In both cases, known orphans' land and fenced trees, the fallen dates are forbidden.

steps.title: רבה: bundles in a public place are the finder's even with a סימן
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about bundles in רשות הרבים. רבה says this applies even if they have a סימן, which shows he holds a סימן likely to be trampled is not a real סימן.
steps.simpleTranslation: Bundles in a public place belong to the finder. רבה said: Even if the item has an identifying mark. So רבה holds that a mark likely to be trampled does not count as a mark.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic by going back to a line in the משנה. It brings רבה's explanation of that line, and then figures out what רבה must hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Many people walk through a public place, so any סימן on the bundles will probably get trampled and ruined. רבה says the owner knows this, does not count on the סימן, and gives up right away. That is why the finder may keep the bundles.

keyTerms.meaning: An identifying mark likely to be trampled

phrases.aramaic: כְּרִיכוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: Bundles in a public area — these belong to him.
phrases.notes: This is a quote from our משנה.

phrases.english: רבה said:
And even with an item that has an identifying mark.
Apparently, רבה holds:

phrases.aramaic: סִימָן הֶעָשׂוּי לִידָּרֵס לָא הָוֵי סִימָן.
phrases.english: A mark likely to be trampled is not a mark.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּרִיכוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ. אָמַר רַבָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to the משנה after the fallen-dates discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bundles in רשות הרבים belong to the finder even if they have a סימן, because a סימן likely to be trampled does not count.

steps.title: רבא: only without a סימן; a trampled סימן still counts
steps.stepSummary: רבא limits the משנה to items without a סימן. If there is a סימן, the finder must announce it, which shows רבא holds that a סימן likely to be trampled still counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: They only taught this about an item with no mark. But with an item that has a mark, he must announce it. So רבא holds that a mark likely to be trampled does count as a mark.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the opposite explanation of the משנה. Then the גמרא spells out what he must hold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, the owner still counts on the סימן even though it may get trampled. So he does not give up, and the finder has to announce what he found. In רבא's view the משנה only lets the finder keep bundles that have no סימן.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up רַבָּה (with a ה, says the סימן does NOT count) and רָבָא (with an א, says it DOES count). The names look almost the same, but they hold opposite views here.

phrases.english: רבא said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן,
phrases.english: They only taught this about an item with no mark,
but with an item that has a mark,
he is obligated to announce it.
Apparently, רבא holds:
A mark likely to be trampled is a mark.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposing reading of the same משנה line that רבה explained in step 18.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה applies only to items without a סימן. With a סימן, the finder must announce it, because a סימן likely to be trampled still counts.

steps.title: A second version: the dispute taught on its own
steps.stepSummary: Some teach the רבה–רבא dispute as a general rule, not attached to the משנה: רבה says a trampled סימן is not a סימן, and רבא says it is.
steps.simpleTranslation: And some teach this teaching on its own: about a mark likely to be trampled, רבה said it is not a mark, and רבא said it is a mark.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another way of teaching the same argument. Here it is a stand-alone rule, not an explanation of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two positions stay the same, but the setting changes. In the first version, the argument comes out of reading the משנה about bundles. In this version, it is a general question about any סימן that is likely to be trampled.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who teach it this way

steps.whatToRemember: רבה: a סימן likely to be trampled is NOT a סימן, so the owner gives up. רבא: it IS a סימן, so the finder must announce. One version ties the dispute to the משנה of bundles, and another teaches it on its own.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּאַנְפֵּי נַפְשַׁהּ:
phrases.english: And there are those who teach this teaching on its own:
phrases.notes: On its own means not as an explanation of the משנה, just as a general rule.

phrases.english: A mark likely to be trampled,
רבה said: It is not a mark,
and רבא said: It is a mark.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיכָּא דְּמַתְנֵי לְהָא שְׁמַעְתָּא בְּאַנְפֵּי נַפְשַׁהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents the dispute of steps 18–19 as a stand-alone teaching instead of a reading of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: About a סימן likely to be trampled, רבה says it is not a סימן and רבא says it is.

steps.title: The bundles ruling seems to refute רבא
steps.stepSummary: A ruling about bundles found in public and private areas seems to show that a סימן likely to be trampled is not a real סימן. That is a challenge against רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: bundles found in a public area belong to the finder. Bundles found in a private area, he takes them and announces them. What is the case? If the bundles have no סימן, what would he announce in a private area? So they must have a סימן. And still it says that in a public area they belong to the finder. This shows a סימן likely to be trampled is not a סימן. That is a refutation of רבא!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ruling about bundles of grain and argues that it proves רבה right and רבא wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The private-area case needs an announcement, so the bundles must have a סימן, otherwise there would be nothing to announce. But the same bundles in a public area go to the finder, even with that סימן. Since bundles in public get stepped on, this suggests a trampled סימן doesn't count, against רבא's view in step 19.

keyTerms.meaning: A public area where many people walk
He takes it and announces that he found it

steps.confusionAlert: The proof works only because of the private-area case. That case shows the bundles have a סימן, and then the public-area case shows that this סימן doesn't help there.

phrases.aramaic: תְּנַן: כְּרִיכוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: We learned: bundles in a public area belong to him (the finder),
in a private area, he takes them and announces.
What is the case?
If there is no identifying mark on them,
then in a private area, what would he announce?
Rather, is it not that there is a mark on them,

phrases.aramaic: וְקָתָנֵי: בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: and it teaches: in a public area, they belong to him.

phrases.aramaic: אַלְמָא סִימָן הֶעָשׂוּי לִידָּרֵס לָא הָוֵי סִימָן,
phrases.english: So apparently a mark likely to be trampled is not a mark,
a refutation of Rava!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the רבה–רבא dispute from step 20 against a ruling about bundles.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's view that a סימן likely to be trampled still counts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The private-area announcement proves the bundles have a סימן. Yet in public the finder keeps them, so a trampled סימן must not count.

steps.title: רבא: no סימן, the announcement is about the place
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the bundles have no סימן at all. In a private area the finder announces so the owner can identify the place where he lost them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא could tell you: really, the bundles have no סימן. And what you asked, 'what would he announce in a private area?' He announces, and the owner identifies the place.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends himself by saying the ruling is about bundles with no סימן, so it says nothing about trampled סימנים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed an announcement only makes sense if there is a סימן. רבא says the owner can prove ownership by naming the exact place (מקום) where he lost the bundles. In a private area few people pass, so the place is reliable, and no other סימן is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Really' — used to keep the original reading and push back on the challenge
The place where the item was lost, used to identify it

phrases.english: Rava could say to you:
Really, there is no mark on them,

phrases.aramaic: וּדְקָא אָמְרַתְּ בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד מַאי מַכְרֵיז?
phrases.english: and as for what you said, in a private area what would he announce?
He announces, for the place.
phrases.notes: He announces what he found, and the owner proves it's his by naming the place where he lost it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָךְ רָבָא: לְעוֹלָם דְּלֵית בְּהוּ סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines the case: no סימן, and the place is what is announced.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The private-area announcement must mean the bundles have a סימן.
steps.terutzMaskana: The bundles have no סימן. The owner identifies them by their מקום, so the ruling proves nothing about trampled סימנים.

steps.title: A second dispute: does a place count as a סימן?
steps.stepSummary: רבה holds that a מקום is not a סימן, so for him רבא's answer wouldn't work. The גמרא shows this is a known dispute between them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה says: a place is not a סימן. As it was stated: about a place, רבה says it is not a סימן, and רבא says it is a סימן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why רבה reads the ruling differently, by quoting a separate dispute between רבה and רבא about whether a place counts as a סימן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא's answer depends on a מקום being a valid סימן. רבה disagrees about that too, so for him the bundles must have a real סימן. This explains why רבה and רבא keep reading the same ruling in opposite ways.
steps.whyThisMatters: Now there are two disputes between רבה and רבא: a trampled סימן, and the place as a סימן. The next ברייתא is read through both.

phrases.aramaic: וְרַבָּה אָמַר: מָקוֹם לָא הָוֵי סִימָן.
phrases.english: And Rabba says: a place is not a mark.
As it was stated: regarding a place,
Rabba says: it is not a mark,
and Rava says: it is a mark.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why רבה would not accept רבא's answer in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבה: a מקום is not a סימן. רבא: a מקום is a סימן.

steps.title: The fuller ruling with sheaves: how does each explain it?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the ruling again with an extra line about large sheaves, which are always announced. Then it asks how רבה and רבא each explain it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: bundles in a public area belong to the finder. In a private area, he takes them and announces. And sheaves, whether in a public area or a private area, he takes them and announces. How does רבה explain this, and how does רבא explain it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a longer version of the ruling, which adds large sheaves, and sets up the question of how each side explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new part is that large sheaves are announced even in a public area, unlike small bundles. Each of them must explain why sheaves differ from bundles according to his own view. The answer comes in the next step.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: כְּרִיכוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: Bundles in a public area belong to him,
in a private area, he takes them and announces.
And sheaves, whether in a public area
or in a private area, he takes them and announces.
How does Rabba explain it,
and how does Rava explain it?

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה הֵיכִי מְתָרֵץ לַהּ, וְרָבָא הֵיכִי מְתָרֵץ לַהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a fuller ruling to see how both sides read it after steps 22–23.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How do רבה and רבא each explain the difference between bundles and sheaves?

steps.title: Each explains it by his own view
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains the ruling as talking about a סימן. רבא explains it as talking about the מקום.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה explains it by his own view, with a סימן. And רבא explains it by his own view, with the place.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the short answer: each one reads the ruling to fit his own opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה the ruling is about bundles with a סימן, because for him a place doesn't count. For רבא it is about identifying by place, since for him a place is a valid סימן. The details come next.

phrases.english: Rabba explains it by his own view, with a mark.
And Rava explains it by his own view, with the place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 24 in short form.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רבה reads the ruling as being about a סימן; רבא reads it as being about the מקום.

steps.title: רבה's explanation begins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts spelling out רבה's reading: bundles in a public area belong to the finder because of... (the text continues past this point).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה explains it by his own view, with a סימן: bundles in a public area belong to the finder, because of...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins walking through the ruling line by line according to רבה. The reason is cut off here and continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה reads the bundles as having a סימן. Still, the finder keeps them in a public area. The reason he is about to give is cut off here.

phrases.english: Rabba explains it by his own view, with a mark:

phrases.aramaic: כְּרִיכוֹת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים – הֲרֵי אֵלּוּ שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: bundles in a public area belong to him,
because of

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Expands רבה's short answer from step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Begins רבה's detailed reading: bundles with a סימן in a public area go to the finder, for a reason that continues next.
